{{ suModeDesc }}

A junction is two statements from independent sources that share one exact value (a name, a figure, a full date or a street address) and each add something the other source never says. Sources that draw on one another or share an outlet are not independent. A pair is left out when any statement in the record already holds both sides, and values carried by many sources are left out as routine. Each junction is a lead to check against the documents, not a finding.

{{ suViewLine }}

You haven't opened any sources yet. Open a few from View a source and this view shows what surprised you, in the order you met it.

The picture is who is in the record, which of them are held together in one statement, and what figure each measure carries. Statements are admitted in the order chosen under Read by, and each is scored by how much it changes that picture at the moment it arrives: a figure that replaces an earlier one, a bond that an earlier statement affirmed and this one negates, two known names held together for the first time. A new name only counts when it is bonded to someone already there. Repeating what is already held moves nothing.

Said in more than one source The same claim made by at least two independent sources, ranked by how unlikely that agreement is given how often its names and words meet anyway. Claims whose numbers or framing differ rank higher. Role lines (“X, director of Y”), citations and bylines are left out, and so is agreement on what most sources say anyway. {{ routineLine }}
